adults.title: When the Numbers Do Not Add Up
adults.big_idea: The law of tithing is a law of faith; as we obey it we show the Lord that we trust Him, and He works in our lives in His own time and way.
adults.objective: Learners will explain in their own words why tithing is a matter of trust more than money, and will choose one way to show the Lord their trust this week.
prepare: Read Elder Giuffra's talk, Trusting the Lord Through Tithes and Offerings, and mark paragraphs 2–10 (the story from Puerto Montt) and 11–13.
Have the talk open on a phone or printed so groups can read from it.
Bring paper and pens for silent writing.
Write on the board: What does my tithing say to the Lord?
Pray for anyone in your class for whom money is a heavy worry right now, and plan to teach gently.

segments.name: Begin: When obedience does not make sense on paper
steps: Invite someone to pray. You may sing or read the words of Because I Have Been Given Much.
Explain that Elder Giuffra of the Seventy admitted that a sister's reasons for not paying tithing made sense from a worldly perspective. Today we look at what he learned.
Ask the first question below. Give pairs one minute each to talk, then take one or two brief responses. Do not ask anyone to share details about money.
questions: When has keeping a commandment looked unreasonable on paper, and what helped you decide what to do?

segments.name: Discover: A sister in Puerto Montt
steps: Form groups of three or four. Ask each group to read paragraphs 2–10 of the talk aloud, changing readers at each paragraph.
Ask groups to look for two turning points: what changed for the young missionary, and what changed for the sister.
Bring the class together. Read aloud the first two key quotes: President Caballero's counsel and the sister's prayer.
Ask the questions below. Let several people answer before you add anything.
questions: Elder Giuffra wondered whether the Lord might have an exception for her. Why do you think his mission president saw an exception as denying her something rather than sparing her?
What do you notice about the way this sister prayed? What did she ask for, and what did she not ask for?

segments.name: Search: The widow and the windows
steps: Explain that President Caballero answered by reading the account of the widow's mite, and that Elder Giuffra closed his talk with Malachi.
Ask half the class to read Mark 12:41–44 in pairs and the other half to read Malachi 3:8, 10 in pairs. Each pair looks for what the passage teaches about the giver's heart and about the Lord.
Invite one pair from each half to report. Then point to the words prove me in Malachi 3:10 and ask the first question below.
Share President Oaks's words that Elder Giuffra quoted (see aligned quotes) and ask the second question.
questions: The Lord invites us to prove Him. What does that invitation tell you about Him?
How has tithing prepared you to keep other covenants, including those made in the house of the Lord?

segments.name: Ponder: Why we obey, and what we can count on
steps: Read the third key quote, the principle Elder Giuffra's wife teaches. Invite the class to turn to John 14:15 and read it silently.
Read paragraph 13 of the talk aloud. Point out that the speaker does not promise freedom from trials; he names financial hardship, illness and loss.
Give two minutes of silent writing on the question on the board: What does my tithing say to the Lord? No one will be asked to share what they wrote.
Ask the question below and invite two or three to answer.
questions: According to paragraph 13, what three things can we be sure of even when we do not understand our trials?

segments.name: Witness: Blessings temporal and spiritual
steps: Read the fourth key quote. Then read Elder Bednar's sentence, which Elder Villanueva quoted at this conference (see aligned quotes).
Invite one or two learners to share briefly a blessing from living this law that they nearly overlooked. Ask them to keep amounts and private details out of it.
As a check for understanding, ask a volunteer to finish this sentence in their own words: Tithing is a law of faith because …

segments.name: Act: Choose how you will show your trust
steps: Explain that Elder Giuffra did not extend a specific assignment; he bore testimony. Invite learners to decide for themselves how to act on it, and show the ideas in the act list.
Ask each person to write one thing they will do this week under what they wrote earlier.
Read Elder Giuffra's testimony that as we obey this law we allow the Lord to work miracles in our lives, often in ways we do not expect. Add your own witness of the Savior.
Tell the class that next week you will begin by asking what they noticed about the Lord's hand when they looked for it.

key_quotes.text: Elder Giuffra, you are no one to deny this sister the blessings of the law of tithing. There are no exceptions to this commandment.
Last night I knelt in prayer and told Heavenly Father that I truly wanted to become a member of His Church and that He would need to help me live this law.
We keep the commandments because we love God, not merely because we hope to receive the blessings that come from obedience.
I testify that the law of tithing is a law of faith. As we obey it, we demonstrate our trust in the Lord and allow Him to work miracles in our lives, often in ways we do not expect.

scriptures.use: Half the class reads it in pairs, looking for what the Savior noticed about the widow and what her gift showed about her heart.
The other half reads it in pairs, marking what the Lord asks and what He promises; then discuss the words prove me as a class.
Read silently after the quote from paragraph 12, to connect keeping commandments with loving the Savior.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Dallin H. Oaks
aligned_quotes.text: Tithe paying is evidence that we accept the law of sacrifice. It also prepares us for the law of consecration and the other higher laws of the celestial kingdom.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder David A. Bednar, quoted by Elder Villanueva
aligned_quotes.text: As we live the law of tithing, we often receive significant but subtle blessings that are not always what we expect and easily can be overlooked

takeaways: Tithing is a law of faith; paying it tells the Lord I trust Him.
We keep the commandments because we love God, not only for the blessings.
The Lord knows my circumstances, honors my obedience, and fulfills His promises in His own time and way.
act: Before you next pay tithing or a fast offering, kneel and tell Heavenly Father in your own words why you are doing it.
If living this law feels beyond you right now, pray as the sister in the story did: tell Heavenly Father what you desire and ask Him to help you live it.
Each evening this week, write down one blessing, temporal or spiritual, that you might otherwise have overlooked.
Read Mark 12:41–44 with someone in your home and talk about what the Savior sees when we give.
music: Because I Have Been Given Much
adapt: At home: read paragraphs 2–10 together around the table, then ask each person to answer the board question aloud or in a journal.
Large class: skip the group reading; ask three readers to read the story from the front, then have people discuss the questions with the person beside them.
Short on time: keep the story, Malachi 3:8, 10, the silent writing and the act segment.

youth.title: Does the Math Have to Work First?
youth.big_idea: Paying tithing is how I show the Lord I trust Him, and He keeps His promises in His own time and way.
youth.objective: Youth will explain why tithing is about trust more than money, and will set one personal goal for how they will live this law with the money they earn or receive.
prepare: Read Elder Giuffra's talk and be ready to tell the story in paragraphs 2–10 in your own words.
Ask youth to bring scriptures or use Gospel Library on their phones, and have the talk open there.
Write three questions on separate slips of paper (see the segment called Honest questions).
Bring paper and pens, and something to write with on the board.

segments.name: Fast start: Pick a side
steps: After a prayer, write a made-up budget on the board for an imaginary person: earns 100 a week; rent, heat and food cost 98.
Say: this person wants to pay tithing. Ask everyone who thinks it is possible to stand on one side of the room and everyone who thinks it is not to stand on the other. No sitting in the middle.
Ask one person from each side to give their reason in one sentence. Do not settle it yet.

segments.name: The story: What would you say?
steps: Tell the first half of the story (paragraphs 2–5): as a young missionary in Puerto Montt, Chile, Elder Giuffra and his companion taught a woman of about 70 who cleaned houses and washed clothes. She told them with great sadness that she earned barely enough for rent, a little firewood and some food, and did not think she could ever pay tithing. Stop there.
Role play: in pairs, one is the missionary and one is a companion asking what they should do now. Give them one minute.
Ask two pairs what they decided. Then tell what happened: he called his mission president, wondering whether the Lord might have an exception for her. Read the first key quote.

Finish the story (paragraphs 7–10): the missionaries fasted and prayed; two days later she told them about her prayer. Read the second key quote. She was baptized that Saturday, and her bishop later said she came every week with her tithing envelope and brought her fast offering on the first Sunday of every month.
questions: Whose faith grew in this story? How can you tell?

segments.name: Scripture search: A widow and a promise
steps: Divide into two teams. Team one opens to Mark 12:41–44, the account the mission president read to Elder Giuffra. Team two opens to Malachi 3:8, 10, which Elder Giuffra quoted.
Give each team three minutes to prepare a headline of eight words or fewer that captures what their passage teaches, plus one detail that surprised them.
Each team shares its headline and detail. The other team may ask one question.
Point out the words prove me in Malachi 3:10 and ask the question below.
questions: The Lord actually invites us to test Him on this. Why do you think He does that with tithing?

segments.name: Honest questions
steps: Hand out the three slips to pairs or small groups: (1) If I pay tithing, will my problems go away? (2) Is tithing a deal I make with God to get things? (3) Does the Lord make exceptions when it is really hard?
Each group finds an answer in Elder Giuffra's own words: question 1 in paragraph 13, question 2 in paragraph 12, question 3 in paragraphs 5–8.
Groups report in under a minute each. For question 1, add Elder Hathaway's sentence from this conference (see aligned quotes).
Be honest that the speaker promises the Lord's help, not an easy life.
questions: Which of these three questions is closest to one you have had? What in the talk helps?

segments.name: What the Lord does
steps: Read paragraph 16 aloud, or ask a strong reader to. Ask youth to listen for every kind of blessing Elder Giuffra says he has witnessed.
List them on the board as youth call them out. Circle the ones that are not about money.

Read Elder Bednar's sentence, which Elder Villanueva quoted at this conference (see aligned quotes). Check for understanding: ask each person to write a six-word sentence that says what tithing really is. Invite a few to read theirs and let the class pick a favorite.
questions: Why might a blessing from tithing be easy to overlook?

segments.name: Act: My own tithing plan
steps: Remind them that Elder Giuffra first paid tithing from summer jobs after his baptism, before he fully understood the promises. Understanding came as he lived and taught it.
Explain that he did not give a specific assignment in this talk, so each person chooses. Show the ideas in the act list and give one minute to write a goal privately.
Read the third key quote as his promise and testimony, and share your own witness that the Savior lives and keeps His word.
Tell them you will start next week by asking who looked for a blessing and what they saw.

key_quotes.text: Elder Giuffra, you are no one to deny this sister the blessings of the law of tithing. There are no exceptions to this commandment.
Last night I knelt in prayer and told Heavenly Father that I truly wanted to become a member of His Church and that He would need to help me live this law.
I testify that the law of tithing is a law of faith. As we obey it, we demonstrate our trust in the Lord and allow Him to work miracles in our lives, often in ways we do not expect.
We keep the commandments because we love God, not merely because we hope to receive the blessings that come from obedience.

scriptures.use: Team one reads it on phones or in scriptures and writes a headline of eight words or fewer about what the Savior saw in the widow's gift.
Team two reads it and writes a headline; then the whole class talks about the Lord's invitation to prove Him.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder David A. Bednar, quoted by Elder Villanueva
aligned_quotes.text: As we live the law of tithing, we often receive significant but subtle blessings that are not always what we expect and easily can be overlooked

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Hathaway
aligned_quotes.text: Some miracles are immediate, some come after long waiting, and some await the Resurrection.

takeaways: Tithing is a law of faith, and paying it shows the Lord I trust Him.
I keep commandments because I love God, not to strike a bargain.
The Lord keeps His promises in His own time and way, often in ways I do not expect.
act: Decide now that tithing comes first out of any money you earn or are given, and set up a simple way to do it (an envelope, a jar, or a note in your phone).
The next time you pay tithing, pray first and tell Heavenly Father why you are paying it.
Keep a list in your phone this week titled Blessings I almost missed and add one line a day.
Ask a parent, leader or returned missionary how they gained their own testimony of tithing.
adapt: At home: do the budget question at the table, tell the story, read Malachi 3:8, 10 together, and let each person set a private goal.
Small class of two or three: skip teams; read both passages together and answer the three honest questions as one group.
Short on time: keep the fast start, the story with both quotes, and the act segment.

children.title: I Can Trust Heavenly Father
children.big_idea: When I pay tithing, I show Heavenly Father that I trust Him.
children.objective: Children will say that paying tithing shows we trust Heavenly Father, and will name one blessing He has given them.
prepare: Read paragraphs 2–10 and 20 of Elder Giuffra's talk so you can tell the story simply.
Cut ten paper circles for coins (or use ten building blocks) and bring an envelope.
Bring paper and crayons for each child.
Be ready to sing Keep the Commandments or My Heavenly Father Loves Me.

segments.name: Welcome and song
steps: Invite a child to pray. Sing Keep the Commandments together.
Ask: who is someone you trust to catch you if you jump? Let a few children answer.
Say: today we will learn one way to show Heavenly Father that we trust Him.

segments.name: Ten coins
steps: Lay the ten paper coins on the floor or table. Count them aloud together.
Explain: everything we have comes from Heavenly Father. He asks us to give one part out of ten back to Him. This is called tithing.
Let a child pick up one coin and put it in the envelope. Count the nine that are left. Let other children take turns doing the same.
Teach the truth with actions and repeat it three times: When I pay tithing (hold out one finger), I show Heavenly Father (point up) that I trust Him (hands on heart).

segments.name: Act out the story
steps: Tell the children that Elder Giuffra, a leader in the Church, told a true story from when he was a missionary in the country of Chile. Invite them to stand and act it out with you.
The missionaries taught a grandmother-aged woman who wanted to be baptized. She worked hard cleaning houses and washing clothes. Pretend to sweep and scrub.
When she learned about tithing, she was worried, because she did not have much money. Show a worried face.
That night she knelt down and prayed. Kneel together. She told Heavenly Father she wanted to belong to His Church and asked Him to help her obey this commandment.
The missionaries felt peace. She was baptized. And every week she came to church with her tithing envelope. March in place holding a pretend envelope.
Ask the questions below.
questions: What did she do when she was worried?
How did she show Heavenly Father that she trusted Him?

segments.name: Jesus sees what we give
steps: Hold up two of the paper coins. Explain that in Mark 12:41–44 Jesus watched people giving money at the temple. A woman gave two very small coins. It was all she had.
Let two children drop the two coins into the envelope while everyone watches quietly.

Say: Jesus saw her. He was glad because she gave with love and trust. Jesus sees us too. Read Elder Fale's words from this conference (see aligned quotes) and invite the children to say them with you.
questions: How do you think the woman felt about Heavenly Father?

segments.name: Windows of heaven
steps: Explain that in the scriptures the Lord promises to open the windows of heaven and bless those who pay tithing (Malachi 3:10).
Play a movement game. When you say tithing, children crouch and pretend to put a coin in an envelope. When you say windows, they jump up and open their arms wide like windows. Go faster and faster.
Sit down. Explain that blessings are not always money. Elder Giuffra said some blessings can be seen and some are felt inside, like peace and hope.
Repeat the truth with actions: When I pay tithing, I show Heavenly Father that I trust Him.

segments.name: Draw a blessing
steps: Give each child paper and crayons. Ask them to draw one blessing Heavenly Father has given them.
As they draw, walk around and ask each child to tell you about the picture.
Invite two or three children to show their pictures. After each one, the class says: Thank you, Heavenly Father.

segments.name: Choose and close
steps: Ask the children to say the truth with actions one more time without your help. This is your check that they have learned it.
Invite each child to choose one thing to do this week from the act list, such as thanking Heavenly Father for a blessing in prayer.
Share your testimony that Jesus Christ lives, that He sees us, and that Heavenly Father keeps His promises. Close with prayer.
Tell them that next week you will ask what blessings they noticed.

key_quotes.text: the law of tithing is a law of faith
the Lord always fulfills His promises
We keep the commandments because we love God

scriptures.use: Tell the account simply with two paper coins; older children can read verses 41–42 aloud from their own scriptures.
Explain the promise of the windows of heaven before the movement game; an older child can find and read the verse.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Fale
aligned_quotes.text: I am a child of God and He loves me.

takeaways: When I pay tithing, I show Heavenly Father that I trust Him.
Jesus sees what I give and is glad when I give with love.
Heavenly Father keeps His promises and blesses me.
act: Say thank you to Heavenly Father in prayer for one blessing each day.
Show your drawing to someone at home and tell them the truth you learned.
When you have money of your own, set aside one part out of ten for tithing first.

adapt.younger: For ages 3–7: use big building blocks instead of paper coins and let every child carry one to the envelope or a box. Keep the story to four actions (scrub, worried face, kneel, march) and do it twice. Shorten the scripture segment to dropping in the two coins, and repeat the truth with actions after every activity. Ask an older child or helper to sit beside the youngest during drawing.
adapt.older: For ages 8–11: ask a child to read Malachi 3:10 aloud and another to read Mark 12:41–44. Let an older child lead the windows game and the coin counting. Ask a harder question: the woman in the story asked Heavenly Father to help her obey; why is that a good prayer when a commandment feels hard? Share Elder Fale's words (see aligned quotes) and ask how knowing Heavenly Father loves us makes it easier to trust Him.
